Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called enrichment non-negotiable. By the fifth round in Rome on May 23, Oman's mediator reported some but not conclusive progress. Witkoff left early. A bipartisan letter signed by 52 senators and 177 representatives warned Trump against any deal allowing Iran to retain any enrichment capability. Talks formally collapsed when Trump, frustrated with the pace, privately issued ultimatums to Tehran and then ordered military strikes without returning to negotiations, bypassing Congress entirely.

existing.description_short: 52 Deaths in ICE Detention: Mortality Rate Highest in 20 Years
existing.description_long: Between January 20, 2025 and June 4, 2026, 52 people died in ICE custody — the highest mortality rate in over two decades and more than double Trump's first term rate, according to a June 2026 Human Rights Watch report titled Dying in Detention. The death rate was nearly four times that of the Biden administration. The Trump administration pushed ICE detention to a record high of 71,000 people by January 2026, up 77% from January 2025, while the annual death rate tripled — a disproportionate increase. In facilities where deaths occurred, populations were on average 242 detainees higher than the 10-year average in the two weeks before each death. Notable cases include Maksym Chernyak, 44, whose detention staff failed to call emergency services for over four and a half hours during a life-threatening emergency. A CNN investigation found many deaths were preventable due to understaffed medical teams, uninterrupted delays in offsite care, and DHS contractor failures. Deaths in 2026 were on track to exceed 2025.

existing.description_short: The Nunes Memo: Patel's Four Pages That Helped Dismantle Trust in the Mueller Investigation
existing.description_long: In January 2018, Kash Patel, then a senior aide to House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes, was the primary drafter of the infamous Nunes Memo — a four-page classified document released on February 2, 2018. The memo alleged that FBI and DOJ officials had committed FISA abuses by concealing the political origins of the Steele dossier from surveillance court judges. The central claim — that the applications did not disclose the DNC's funding of the Steele research — was flatly contradicted by the actual FISA application, which contained a lengthy footnote disclosing the politically-motivated origins. The New York Times later reported that many of the flaws Patel claimed turned out to be false or misleading. While DOJ Inspector General Horowitz's 2019 report did find 17 significant errors in the FISA applications, the specific claims in Patel's memo were largely wrong or cherry-picked. The memo nonetheless served its political purpose: galvanizing Trump supporters, delegitimizing the Mueller investigation, and launching Patel's career as a MAGA national security celebrity.

Within weeks, more than 130 CISA employees overall were fired, including 10 regional specialists who liaised directly with state and local election offices. Acting CISA director Bridget Bean issued a Valentine's Day memo defunding the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center (EI-ISAC), a nationwide program providing threat monitoring to state election officials. The memo ordered a review of every election security position and program dating back to Trump's first term. Attorney General Pam Bondi on February 5 separately disbanded the FBI task force on election threats against election workers. Democrats on the Senate and House oversight committees warned the moves left states without federal protection against ransomware and foreign cyberattacks ahead of the 2026 midterms. Former officials said the cuts specifically targeted staff who had monitored Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence operations in the 2024 election cycle.

existing.title: DOJ Sues 30+ States Demanding Detailed Voter Registration Databases
existing.description_short: DOJ Sues 30+ States Demanding Detailed Voter Registration Databases
existing.description_long: Beginning in mid-2025 and escalating through 2026, the Department of Justice launched an unprecedented campaign to compel all 50 states and the District of Columbia to turn over detailed voter registration databases containing voters' full names, dates of birth, residential addresses, driver's license numbers, and last four digits of Social Security numbers. The DOJ pursued this under a confidential memorandum of understanding framework citing EO 14248. By May 2026, the DOJ had filed lawsuits against 30 states and D.C. that refused. By July 2026, courts had ruled against the DOJ in all 16 federal court decisions issued on the matter, with a Rhode Island judge calling it a fishing expedition and seven of the 15 district court judges who ruled against Trump having been appointed by Trump himself. Even Republican-controlled states including Idaho, Utah, West Virginia, and Kentucky resisted, citing privacy concerns. Critics warned the consolidated database would create a federal surveillance tool over American voters. Democratic states described it as an attempt to nationalize elections in violation of the Constitution's elections clause.

existing.description_short: LGBTQ Federal Employees Targeted in DEI Purge and Firings
existing.description_long: Beginning January 20, 2025, Trump's executive orders on DEI and 'gender ideology' immediately placed employees whose roles involved 'promoting gender ideology' on paid administrative leave with computer access cut off, and at least six EOs directly targeted LGBTQ people in the federal workforce. The Williams Institute estimated approximately 314,000 LGBTQ employees of the federal government, USPS, and federal contractors were exposed to displacement. An OPM memo in early February directed agencies to prohibit employee resource groups promoting 'DEIA initiatives,' and OPM opened a tipline for workers to report colleagues involved in DEI activities — drawing comparisons to the 1950s 'Lavender Scare.' Trump also rescinded a nearly 60-year-old executive order (EO 11246) on January 21, 2025 prohibiting discrimination by federal contractors, removing protections for roughly 100,000 LGBTQ contractor employees. The Department of Homeland Security announced it would allow its agents to conduct surveillance based solely on a target's gender identity or sexual orientation. On March 26, 2025, a class-action complaint was filed before the Merit Systems Protection Board on behalf of fired federal DEI employees.

original_title: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub

existing.title: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
existing.description_short: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
existing.description_long: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent a letter to Federal Election Commission Chair Ellen Weintraub — a Democratic commissioner who had been an outspoken critic of Trump's campaign finance violations — stating You are hereby removed as a Member of the Federal Election Commission, effective immediately. Weintraub publicly rejected the removal as illegal, noting that no president had ever fired an FEC commissioner and that the Federal Election Campaign Act contained no firing authority for the president. Republican former FEC Chair Trevor Potter called the action contrary to law, noting that Trump was free to nominate a replacement but could not simply fire a sitting commissioner. The timing was significant: the FEC was preparing to consider complaints against Trump's 2024 campaign and against Elon Musk's $277 million in political spending. Weintraub lost her email, computer, and cellphone access by February 7. The move was part of a broader pattern of firing independent agency members and preceded the eventual July 2026 Supreme Court ruling that gave presidents expanded power to fire independent agency members.

existing.description_short: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process
existing.description_long: On March 15–16, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act — not used since World War II — to deport 137 Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador's CECOT prison with no notice, no hearings, and no opportunity to challenge removal. Federal Judge James Boasberg had issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, and evidence emerged that planes carrying detainees had been ordered to continue to El Salvador even after the TRO was issued. In June 2025, Boasberg ruled in a sweeping opinion that the men had been plainly deprived of due process rights, comparing their situation to a Kafka novel: Perhaps the President lawfully invoked the Alien Enemies Act. Perhaps, moreover, Defendants are correct that Plaintiffs are gang members. But there is simply no way to know for sure, as the CECOT Plaintiffs never had any opportunity to challenge the Government's say-so. The Supreme Court unanimously agreed the men were entitled to notice and the opportunity to challenge removal before deportation. The administration had given some detainees as little as 24 hours notice.

The Senate Intelligence Committee later concluded in 2020 that Manafort's sharing of internal polling data with a Russian associate with GRU ties constituted a grave counterintelligence threat.

original_title: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists

existing.title: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
existing.description_short: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
existing.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order gutting the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), Voice of America's parent. By the morning of March 15, all 1,300 VOA employees had been placed on paid administrative leave, barred from the building and their equipment. DOGE operative Gavin Kliger — a former Twitter engineer — had been spotted inside VOA headquarters weeks earlier. VOA director Michael Abramowitz stated: For the first time in 83 years, the storied Voice of America is being silenced. Kari Lake, Trump's loyalist USAGM adviser, signed termination notices and canceled the agency's 15-year lease. VOA had operated continuously since 1942, originally to counter Nazi propaganda, and reached an estimated 247 million people weekly in 47 languages. Russian state media celebrated the shutdown; China's state press called VOA a dirty rag. The National Press Club said the action undermines America's long-standing commitment to a free press. Courts had blocked similar USAGM dismantlement attempts during Trump's first term. The shutdown left audiences across authoritarian states without access to independent, U.S.-funded journalism precisely when such coverage mattered most.

No evidence of widespread 2020 voter fraud has been found by any investigation, including those conducted by Trump-appointed officials.

existing.description_long: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, flanked by Republican lawmakers at EPA headquarters, proposed repealing all greenhouse gas emissions standards for the U.S. power sector under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act — effectively eliminating both the 2015 Obama-era standards for new fossil fuel plants and Biden's 2024 Clean Power Plan 2.0 emission guidelines for existing coal, oil, and gas plants. The proposal also moved to repeal 2024 amendments to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards that had been requiring coal plants to reduce brain-damaging mercury emissions. Zeldin claimed the rollbacks would save $120 million per year for electric utilities. Environmental groups countered that the repeals would increase cancer-causing and neurotoxic air pollution, lock in decades of carbon emissions, and kill thousands of Americans prematurely each year from worsened air quality. EPA had telegraphed the move on March 12, 2025, when Zeldin announced it as part of what he called the most consequential day of deregulation in U.S. history. A public hearing on the GHG repeal was held July 8, 2025, with EPA planning to finalize the rule by spring 2026.

Companies like Jordan Manufacturing in Belding, Michigan, saw steel prices rise 5%–10% and were forced to raise customer prices 8%–14%. The Tax Foundation's Erica York said: It's just very foolish to double down on this type of tariff in particular. Canada's steel and aluminum industry faced mass layoffs and investment deferrals. U.S. construction contracted 3.6% in long-run projections from the Yale Budget Lab.

original_title: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased

existing.title: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased
existing.description_short: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased
existing.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed H.J.Res. 35 — a Congressional Review Act joint resolution — into law as Public Law 119-2, nullifying EPA's Waste Emissions Charge rule that had imposed a $900-per-ton fee on oil and gas producers releasing excess methane, a fee that would have escalated to $1,500 per ton by 2026. The WEC had been a centerpiece of the Inflation Reduction Act's climate provisions, representing the first-ever federal price on methane pollution, which traps 80 times more heat per molecule than CO2 over a 20-year period. existing.description_short: Trump Guts Wildfire Prevention Funding Weeks After Los Angeles Burns
existing.description_long: In the weeks immediately following the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires — expected to be the costliest in U.S. history with losses potentially reaching $35 billion — the Trump administration froze wildfire prevention funding, fired thousands of firefighting-adjacent personnel, and halted seasonal firefighter hiring across the country. By February 13-14, 2025, reports confirmed that the administration had frozen all remaining funds from the $3 billion in wildfire mitigation money appropriated through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and Inflation Reduction Act, canceling contracts with non-profits like the Oregon-based Lomakatsi Restoration Project. On February 15, 2025, the New York Times reported that 3,400 U.S. Forest Service employees — roughly 10% of the agency's workforce — had been terminated, eliminating trail crews, fuel-reduction specialists, and training instructors who form the backbone of wildfire preparedness. A planned 151,434-acre prescribed burn in Everglades National Park was canceled; training programs for forest firefighters were scrapped mid-season; and seasonal hiring stalled just as fire season approached. Federal firefighters told ProPublica that it's always cheaper to do a prescribed burn than to fight an escaped wildfire, while the annual area burned by U.S. wildfires over the past decade was already 43% larger than the historical average tracked since 1983.

Despite absorbing billions in losses, automakers held prices stable through mid-2025 to avoid customer backlash, meaning the full consumer price impact had not yet materialized.

The letters stated explicitly that the officials could not be trusted to faithfully implement the President's agenda because of their significant role in prosecuting the president. Separately, approximately 40 prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia who had worked on January 6 cases were fired the same week. The fired prosecutors received no advance notice. Three FBI agents — Michelle Ball, Jamie Garman, and Blaire Toleman — later sued the administration in March 2025, alleging they were terminated in a retribution campaign for their work on the 2020 election investigation.

original_title: Education Dept. Strips Transgender Student Protections Under Title IX

existing.title: Education Dept. Strips Transgender Student Protections Under Title IX
existing.description_short: Education Dept. Strips Transgender Student Protections Under Title IX
existing.description_long: On January 31, 2025, the U.S. Department of Education issued a Dear Colleague letter signed by Acting Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Craig Trainor announcing that Title IX sex discrimination law would be enforced using the 2020 rules developed under Betsy DeVos during Trump's first term. The move eliminated the Biden administration's 2024 Title IX regulations, which had explicitly protected transgender students' rights to use bathrooms and locker rooms aligned with their gender identity and prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in federally funded schools. The guidance directed that all open Title IX investigations initiated under the 2024 rules should be immediately reoriented to comply with the 2020 framework, which treated sex as binary and provided no protections for gender identity. This followed Trump's first-day executive order declaring the U.S. recognizes only two sexes. Trainor specifically rejected the legal argument, based on the Supreme Court's Bostock decision, that Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination extends to gender identity or sex stereotypes. The practical effect was immediate: transgender students at thousands of schools lost federal civil rights protections against harassment and discrimination. The guidance also raised questions about how the Education Department would handle sexual assault complaints, as the 2020 rules had been criticized for placing higher burdens of proof on assault survivors.

original_title: Trump Kills Biden EV Mandates and Guts CAFE Fuel Economy Standards

existing.title: Trump Kills Biden EV Mandates and Guts CAFE Fuel Economy Standards
existing.description_short: Trump Kills Biden EV Mandates and Guts CAFE Fuel Economy Standards
existing.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order revoking Biden's 2021 goal of 50% EV sales by 2030 and freezing $5 billion in unspent EV charging infrastructure funds, while directing EPA to reconsider emissions rules that would have required 30-56% EV sales by 2032. Then on December 3, 2025, the Trump administration proposed slashing the Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards from Biden's 50.4 miles-per-gallon fleet average target for 2031 down to 34.5 mpg — a 32% rollback that the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's own analysis said would increase fuel consumption by roughly 100 billion gallons through 2050, costing Americans up to $185 billion more in gas expenses over that period. The White House called the CAFE reset delivering a win for American families, claiming it would lower car sticker prices by about $930. In June 2025, Trump signed a joint resolution ending California's authority to set its own stricter EV standards — effectively nullifying similar rules in 17 other states — and in July 2025 Congress zeroed out civil penalties for automakers that violate CAFE rules. Environmental and public health advocates warned the combined rollbacks would dramatically increase greenhouse gas emissions, deepen U.S. oil dependence, and set the domestic auto industry back by a decade compared to European and Chinese competitors.

original_title: HHS Rescinds ACA Section 1557 LGBTQ Healthcare Protections

existing.title: HHS Rescinds ACA Section 1557 LGBTQ Healthcare Protections
existing.description_short: HHS Rescinds ACA Section 1557 LGBTQ Healthcare Protections
existing.description_long: On May 14, 2025, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services formally rescinded four guidance documents, including the critical 2021 interpretation of Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act that had extended healthcare nondiscrimination protections to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. The 2021 guidance had been grounded in the Supreme Court's Bostock v. Clayton County ruling, which held that discrimination based on sex encompasses discrimination against LGBTQ+ individuals under Title VII. The rescission meant that HHS would no longer expect healthcare entities receiving federal funding — including hospitals, insurance plans, and medical providers — to extend nondiscrimination protections to patients based on their sexual orientation or gender identity. In February 2025, HHS had already withdrawn its 2022 guidance on gender-affirming care, and the Justice Department had notified the Supreme Court in Skrmetti v. US that the federal government no longer maintained that prohibitions on transgender healthcare violate the Equal Protection Clause — effectively abandoning transgender people as a protected class. The cascading effect was significant: dozens of hospitals paused gender-affirming services citing legal uncertainty. Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Children's National in Washington D.C., UPMC in Pittsburgh, and Children's Hospital of Los Angeles all scaled back services even where state law permitted them, creating a chilling effect beyond what any individual state ban had achieved.

existing.description_long: On February 5, 2025 — coinciding with National Girls and Women in Sports Day — Trump signed the executive order Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports, directing federal agencies to enforce a ban on transgender women and girls competing in female-designated school sports under a reinterpreted Title IX. The order threatened to cut off all federal funding to any school allowing transgender women or girls to compete in female sports. Despite the sweeping framing, the NCAA president had testified before Congress in December 2024 that he was aware of fewer than 10 transgender athletes among the 530,000 competing at 1,100 member schools — making the executive action an enormous policy hammer targeting a vanishingly small population. The order directed the Department of Justice to ensure all government agencies enforce the sports ban and instructed the Department of Education to change its Title IX enforcement interpretation accordingly. The following day, the Education Department opened a Title IX investigation into the University of Pennsylvania over swimmer Lia Thomas, who had competed for Penn and won the 2022 NCAA championship in the women's 500-yard freestyle — three years before the order was signed. Scores of state-level sports bans were already in effect across Republican-controlled states, meaning the federal order functioned primarily as a funding coercion tool against the remaining schools that had maintained inclusive policies.

existing.description_short: Admin Defies Court Order, Illegally Deports Kilmar Abrego Garcia
existing.description_long: On March 12, 2025, DHS agents arrested Kilmar Abrego Garcia — a Maryland father of three with no criminal record — during a routine traffic stop, giving his wife ten minutes to collect their five-year-old child with disabilities before handing the boy to Child Protective Services. Three days later, despite a 2019 immigration judge's withholding order specifically barring his removal to El Salvador, Abrego Garcia was flown to CECOT, El Salvador's notorious terrorism mega-prison. The government acknowledged the removal was an administrative error. Federal courts ordered his return. On April 10, 2025, the Supreme Court ruled 9-0 that the administration must facilitate his return to the United States, affirming the deportation was illegal. The administration refused to comply in good faith, with DHS filing a declaration claiming it had no authority to secure his return. In an Oval Office meeting, Trump hosted Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, who publicly refused to return Abrego Garcia. Trump then made a veiled threat, commenting to Bukele: Homegrown criminals next. Justice Sotomayor warned in a concurrence that the government's position implied it could deport and imprison any person — including U.S. citizens — without legal consequence. As of December 2025, Abrego Garcia had been returned to the U.S. but a federal judge was still blocking his re-detainment, saying she did not trust the administration not to illegally deport him again.

existing.description_long: In July 2026, the Trump Justice Department issued grand jury subpoenas to at least three New York Times journalists who had reported on security concerns with Trump's Qatar-gifted Air Force One jet, seeking to compel them to testify about their confidential sources — and then issued additional subpoenas to third-party phone carriers for the reporters' phone and text records, extending to spouses of two reporters and the mother of a third, a step legal experts called extraordinarily aggressive and unorthodox. Attorney General Pam Bondi had earlier in 2025 revoked DOJ policies protecting journalists from subpoenas — policies established after abuses under prior administrations — explicitly to enable aggressive pursuit of government leakers.

original_title: ICE Raids Ventura County Farms, 70% of Agricultural Workforce Flees

existing.title: ICE Raids Ventura County Farms, 70% of Agricultural Workforce Flees
existing.description_short: ICE Raids Ventura County Farms, 70% of Agricultural Workforce Flees
existing.description_long: In early June 2025, ICE agents conducted sweeping raids across farms and packinghouses in Ventura County, California — one of the most productive agricultural regions in the United States, producing billions of dollars of strawberries, celery, and other crops annually. Community organizers reported at least 35 people arrested in the raids. Immediately following the raids, eyewitnesses described fields falling eerily silent: workers who would normally be moving through rows of crops were gone, farm entry gates were locked, and the landscape that had been full of labor was empty. Lisa Tate, a sixth-generation Ventura County farmer, told Reuters: In the fields, I would say 70% of the workers are gone. If 70% of your workforce doesn't show up, 70% of your crop doesn't get picked and can go bad in one day. Most Americans don't want to do this work. Most farmers here are barely breaking even. I fear this has created a tipping point where many will go bust. Similar raids followed in other agricultural communities: eleven workers arrested at Outlook Dairy Farms in New Mexico; eight dairy workers arrested at Pleasant Valley Farms in Vermont; and Indigenous Guatemalan farmworkers arrested near Woodburn, Oregon while traveling to a blueberry farm. In each community, advocates described empty streets, shuttered businesses, and widespread panic. The raids left crops unharvested and raised urgent warnings about disruption to the US food supply chain.

The Sanchez case occurred within days of the V.M.L. deportation case and the deportation of three US citizen children to Honduras, suggesting a systematic pattern rather than isolated errors. Pediatric health advocates noted the sudden cessation of breastfeeding posed significant health risks to the infant daughter.

existing.description_short: Trump Launches $TRUMP Memecoin Three Days Before Inauguration
existing.description_long: On January 17, 2025, three days before his second inauguration, Donald Trump launched the $TRUMP memecoin through CIC Digital LLC, a Trump Organization affiliate. Within hours the token's market capitalization surged above $9 billion, briefly making it one of the most valuable meme coins in crypto history, with a peak price of $75.35. By early July 2026 the token was trading at roughly $1.69, down 98% from its peak. Trump's 2025 annual financial disclosure, a 927-page document released in June 2026, reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto-related income for his first year back in the White House, mostly from World Liberty Financial token sales and memecoin royalties — making crypto his family's single largest business interest, surpassing real estate. Ethics experts called it an unprecedented concentration of financial interest inside a presidency that was simultaneously writing the rules governing the same industry.

EFF noted that Trump had already 'frequently targeted platforms carrying content and speakers of entirely legal speech that is critical of him' through frivolous lawsuits against media defendants. The organization warned that the hastily drafted, overbroad bill would 'threaten to silence critics and draw scarce resources away from important reporting work' while Trump openly declared his intention to use it for censorship rather than its stated purpose of protecting victims.

Ethics experts noted that the pattern — financial criminals whose families had paid into Trump's fundraising apparatus receiving clemency while their fraud victims received nothing — constituted corruption so naked it had no precedent in modern American presidential history.

Customs and Border Protection agents stopped him at a Texas airport. ICE had flagged two prior convictions — a 2006 failure to stop for a police officer and a 2019 disorderly conduct charge — as potential grounds for deportation. Crayk publicly noted that every day of Dioses's detention was paid for by taxpayers on charges the government itself ultimately acknowledged were invalid.

original_title: Family Separation Policy - 'Zero Tolerance' Child Abuse

existing.title: Family Separation Policy - 'Zero Tolerance' Child Abuse
existing.description_short: Family Separation Policy - 'Zero Tolerance' Child Abuse
existing.description_long: In April 2018, Donald Trump's administration implemented a 'zero tolerance' immigration policy that systematically separated thousands of migrant children from their parents at the U.S.-Mexico border, creating what human rights experts called a humanitarian crisis and form of state-sponsored child abuse. The policy, announced by Attorney General Jeff Sessions, criminally prosecuted all adults crossing the border illegally, including asylum seekers, which resulted in children being taken from their parents and placed in detention facilities, foster care, or with sponsors across the country. Over 2,600 children were separated from their families, including infants and toddlers, with many held in overcrowded facilities that resembled cages. Audio recordings from detention facilities captured children crying for their parents, with one recording featuring a 6-year-old begging for her 'Papá.' Trump initially denied responsibility for the separations, falsely claiming they were required by law and blaming Democrats. When confronted with overwhelming criticism, Trump defended the policy as necessary deterrent, with officials like former Chief of Staff John Kelly stating the separations would deter future immigration. After weeks of international condemnation and legal challenges, Trump signed an executive order ending family separations on June 20, 2018, while falsely claiming credit for solving a problem his own administration created. Many families remained separated for months or years afterward, with some parents deported without their children. The Trump administration had no system in place to reunite families, leading to prolonged trauma for both children and parents.

existing.title: DOJ Drops Peter Navarro Records Lawsuit, Stops Defending Contempt Conviction
existing.description_short: DOJ Drops Peter Navarro Records Lawsuit, Stops Defending Contempt Conviction
existing.description_long: Peter Navarro, Trump's trade adviser, had been convicted in September 2023 of two misdemeanor contempt of Congress counts for defying a subpoena from the January 6 House Select Committee and served four months in federal prison in 2024. On June 4, 2025, the Trump DOJ abruptly dropped the long-running civil lawsuit it had filed in 2022 seeking to recover hundreds of presidential records Navarro had retained on a personal ProtonMail account — dismissing the case with prejudice and with no explanation, despite the Supreme Court having refused to hear Navarro's appeal of the records production order in December 2024 and a magistrate judge having just reviewed over 1,800 emails. Then in September 2025, the DOJ stopped defending Navarro's criminal contempt conviction before the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, filing a statement that it no longer shared the prior administration's legal position. The D.C. Circuit declined to appoint outside counsel to defend the conviction. After the Supreme Court returned the case to the district court in April 2026, the DOJ's motion to dismiss the criminal indictment was moving forward for final resolution. Navarro — who had returned to the White House as senior counselor for trade and manufacturing and became one of the chief architects of Trump's second-term tariff policy — described his prosecution in a memoir as I Went to Prison so You Won't Have To: A Love and Lawfare Story in Trump Land. His ally Bannon's case was resolved identically.
